title: Command pattern
idea: The Command pattern turns a request into an object with an `execute` method, so you can queue it, log it, retry it or undo it later.

analogy.text: A waiter writes your order on a ticket and pins it to the kitchen rail. The cook works through tickets; the waiter never cooks.
analogy.breaks: A paper ticket cannot reverse itself; a command can undo.

points: A command bundles the receiver, the action and its arguments into one object.
The invoker runs commands through one interface and keeps them for undo or replay.
A `Runnable` given to an `ExecutorService` is a command: a request run later elsewhere.
Skip it for a direct call nobody queues, logs or undoes; it adds classes.

hero.title: Undo and redo stacks over seven clicks

steps.caption: The inventory starts empty. Both history stacks are empty.
`run` executes the command on the receiver, then pushes it on the undo stack.
Removing 4 is another command object. It carries its own inverse: add 4 back.
Removing 50 throws inside the receiver. `run` catches it and records nothing.
`undo` pops the newest command, calls its `undo`, and parks it on the redo stack.
`redo` executes the very same object again and moves it back. Nothing was copied.
Undo once more: remove 4 waits on the redo stack again.
A new command clears the redo stack. Replaying remove 4 now would rewrite a different past.

code.title: The problem: direct calls
code.caption: The screen calls the store directly and remembers only its last change.

walk.text: No request objects: the screen mutates the map and keeps two fields of history.
Each change overwrites the previous record, so all older history is lost.
Undo applies the inverse of that one change, and never clears it.
The second undo reverses `nut` again. Stock goes negative and `bolt` is never restored.

code.title: The fix: command objects
code.caption: Each click becomes an immutable command; an invoker keeps undo and redo stacks.

walk.text: The receiver does the real work and guards its own rule: no negative stock.
One small interface. The invoker sees only `execute`, `undo` and `name`.
A command is a record: receiver plus arguments, validated once, with its exact inverse.
`run` records a command only after it succeeds. A failed one never enters history.
A new action clears the redo stack, so redo cannot replay a stale branch.
Undo and redo move the same object between two stacks; no state is copied.
`Runnable` is the JDK's own command interface: each click here is a request object.

pitfalls: Pushing a command before `execute` succeeds lets undo reverse a change that never happened.
Not clearing the redo stack on a new action lets redo corrupt the current state.
Commands that hold mutable arguments change when the caller reuses them; make commands immutable.

quiz.q: Same classes as the demo. What does the last line print?
quiz.why: Undo leaves 5. The new `add 1` makes 6 and clears the redo stack, so `redo` finds nothing and returns false.

takeaway: A command is a request as an object: run it, store it, undo it.

starters: When should undo store an inverse command instead of a Memento snapshot?
